Keep On Truckin'
keep on TRUK-in
catchphrase (Boomer-era slang)
From 1930s blues/jazz ("truckin'" as a dance and keep-moving idiom) revived by R. Crumb's 1968 one-page comic of strutting big-footed walkers; through the 1970s it meant: persist, keep going, carry on through the grind.

📖 Biblical Definition

Keep on truckin' is the Boomer era's one-line theology of persistence: whatever the road serves up, keep moving. Born in 1930s blues idiom and rebooted by R. Crumb's strutting 1968 cartoon — plastered across vans, t-shirts, and mudflaps for a decade — it functioned as a grinning, secular benediction: don't quit. The dictionary receives this one warmly, because its instinct is among the most biblical in all of slang. Scripture's ethics of the long road are exactly this, with the engine named: let us not be weary in well doing: for in due season we shall reap, if we faint not (Gal 6:9); let us run with patience the race that is set before us (Heb 12:1); I press toward the mark (Phil 3:14); and the old man's victory lap, I have fought a good fight, I have finished my course (2 Tim 4:7). The one correction the gospel makes to the mudflap is the fuel source: the believer's truckin' is not gritted-teeth self-propulsion but looking unto Jesus (Heb 12:2), strength supplied by the One who never wearies (Isa 40:28-31). Direction matters too — persistence on the broad road is just efficient ruin. Point the truck at the mark, then by all means: keep on.

📜 Origin & Era

Blues idiom + R. Crumb's 1968 comic: the era's grinning benediction of persistence. Nearly straight Bible — Gal 6:9, Heb 12:1, Phil 3:14 — once the fuel (looking unto Jesus) and the direction are set. Verdict: redeemable.

KEEP ON TRUCKIN', catchphrase (Boomer era; blues 1930s, revived 1968) Persist; keep going; carry on through the grind.

Blues/jazz lineage: "truckin'" as a dance and keep-moving idiom (1930s).

R. Crumb's 1968 one-page comic of strutting walkers makes it a decade's emblem.

Vans, t-shirts, mudflaps: the 1970s' secular benediction.

Gospel corrections: fuel (looking unto Jesus) and direction (the mark, not the broad road).

📖 Key Scripture

Gal 6:9 — "And let us not be weary in well doing: for in due season we shall reap, if we faint not."

Heb 12:1 — "Wherefore seeing we also are compassed about with so great a cloud of witnesses, let us lay aside every weight, and the sin which doth so easily beset us, and let us run with patience the race that is set before us,"

Phil 3:14 — "I press toward the mark for the prize of the high calling of God in Christ Jesus."

2 Tim 4:7 — "I have fought a good fight, I have finished my course, I have kept the faith:"

⚠️ Modern Corruption

Scarcely corrupted — the rare slang whose instinct is nearly straight Bible. The two gospel amendments: persistence needs a fuel source better than grit, and a direction better than the broad road.

expand to see more

Grit and its limits. The mudflap version runs on self-propulsion, and self-propulsion runs out — ask any Boomer who white-knuckled the long road into burnout or a bottle. The biblical long-haul has a named engine: they that wait upon the LORD shall renew their strength... they shall walk, and not faint (Isa 40:31), and the race is run looking unto Jesus, the author and finisher (Heb 12:2). Perseverance of the saints is not the saints' grip on God but God's grip on the saints — which is why it actually finishes.

Largely innocent era-slang; the principle to add is direction. Persistence is a multiplier, not a virtue by itself: keep on truckin' down the broad way and you merely arrive at destruction ahead of schedule (Matt 7:13). Scripture's persistence verses all carry a vector — well doing, the race SET BEFORE US, the mark, the faith KEPT. Point the truck first; then the old benediction is gospel: in due season we shall reap, if we faint not.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

1930s blues idiom revived by R. Crumb's 1968 comic into the 1970s' benediction of persistence; nearly straight Bible (Gal 6:9; Heb 12:1) once fuel and direction are gospel-set.
